opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a single moment. It was more a gradual realization that the project had outgrown what we could support purely as an academic open-source effort.

SGLang started in a research setting. We were trying to solve real problems in LLM serving, like how to reuse the KV cache efficiently across requests, which is where RadixAttention came from, and how to make structured generation and complex programs fast. We open-sourced it because we believed the ideas should be available to everyone. Then adoption grew much faster than we expected. Companies started running it in production at very large scale, and the community of contributors kept expanding.

At that point we saw a gap. People running inference seriously need much more than a good open-source engine. They need reliability, fast support for new models and hardware, deployment tooling, and someone accountable when things break at three in the morning. A loose group of researchers and volunteers can only stretch so far. We were getting requests we simply couldn't serve well.

We also believe inference is becoming one of the most important layers in the AI stack. As models get deployed everywhere, and especially as agentic workloads multiply the number of calls, the cost and efficiency of serving becomes a core economic question. We felt we had both the technical depth and the community trust to build something meaningful there.

So RadixArk was really about making SGLang sustainable. We wanted a dedicated team that could keep pushing performance while staying committed to open source. The open-source project stays at the center. The company exists so it can keep growing and serve the people depending on it.

r001.rationale: The response says adoption grew quickly, companies used SGLang at large scale, and users made requests the team could not support well, attributing the decision to incoming demand.

r002.rationale: It says SGLang began in a research setting and was open-sourced, but does not describe a transition from university research into a purely community project.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, the decision came in stages rather than as a single moment.

SGLang started as a research project. We were trying to solve a very concrete problem: serving large language models fast, with good hardware utilization, and with a programming model that made complex inference workflows easy to express. RadixAttention, the prefix caching idea, came out of that. For a long time we were happy for it to live as an open-source project under LMSYS, with contributions from the community and from people at labs and companies who needed it.

What changed was the scale of who was depending on it. We started seeing SGLang in production at companies serving real traffic, and the requests coming in were no longer just "this kernel is slow" or "this model isn't supported." They were things like "we need this to be reliable across a thousand GPUs," "we need enterprise support," "we need someone accountable when it breaks at three in the morning." An academic project run by a handful of maintainers in their spare time cannot really make those promises, no matter how good the code is.

The second thing was that inference itself became the bottleneck for the whole field. Training gets a lot of attention, but once models are deployed, most of the compute and most of the cost goes into inference. Serving long-context, agentic, multi-turn workloads efficiently is a genuinely hard systems problem, and it was clear it would need a team working on it full time, with the resources to test on real hardware at real scale. That was not going to happen on grant funding.

So RadixArk was really about creating a home where the core team could work on this seriously, keep the open-source project healthy, and also build the layer on top that enterprises actually need. I did not want the open-source side to suffer. If anything, having a company behind it means more engineers maintaining it, not fewer.

And personally, I think there was a sense that if we did not do it, someone else would build a company on our work anyway, and they might not care about the community in the same way. It felt better to be the ones responsible for it.

r001.rationale: The response says production users depended on SGLang and describes incoming requests for reliability, enterprise support, and accountability.

r002.rationale: It says SGLang began as a research project and later lived as an open-source project under LMSYS with community contributions, but does not describe a transition from university research into a purely community project.

astra-6.text:
For me, the key question was how to turn a research project into something people could reliably use in production. With an inference system like SGLang, performance is essential, but it’s only part of the problem. You also need reliability, operational tooling, and ongoing support as models and hardware change.

That was the motivation for establishing RadixArk: to build a dedicated team around that broader problem. Open-source development and a commercial company can serve complementary roles. The open-source project gives people a foundation they can use and contribute to, while the company can take responsibility for helping customers run it in production.

So I’d describe the decision as moving from developing the technology to building an organization that could sustain it and make it useful more broadly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making SGLang useful in production and supporting customers, but does not say incoming requests or demand prompted the commercialization decision.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the roles of open-source development and the company, but does not describe SGLang’s early transition from university research into a purely community project.

sol-6.1.text:
For us, it was less about deciding that SGLang was ready to become a company and more about seeing what people needed around it. An open-source project can give you powerful technology, but running inference in production takes much more: reliability, operational tooling, support, and continued optimization as models and hardware change.

We saw an opportunity to close that gap with RadixArk—to help turn advances in inference systems into something teams could actually deploy and depend on. And we wanted a sustainable way to keep investing in that work while continuing to build the open-source ecosystem.

r001.rationale: It says they saw what people needed around SGLang and an opportunity to help teams deploy it, conveying demand from prospective users.

r002.rationale: It discusses the open-source ecosystem but does not describe SGLang’s early transition from university research into a purely community project.
